instructions:
Read the paper below and produce a structured summary.

It matched these tracked topics; `relevance` must contain one entry per slug, stating what this paper changes for that topic:
- overthinking: Overthinking — When and why large reasoning models think more than a problem needs (or less than it needs) — the accuracy/efficiency tradeoff of reasoning length, test-time compute scaling, and methods to make a model stop, or keep going, at the right point.

Answer `models` explicitly, even when the answer is `[]`. List the checkpoints the work trains, evaluates or analyses, named as the paper names them — a base model, a released model, a judge. A paper that evaluates none returns an empty list, and that is a real answer: the archive holds several. Leaving it out looks identical to that in the record, and nothing afterwards can tell the two apart.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

concepts: string - reusable ideas this paper relies on or introduces
datasets: string - datasets, benchmarks, corpora or simulators used. Not models: a checkpoint that was evaluated or fine-tuned belongs in `models`.
output_schema.limitations: string - stated limits plus any the reader should notice
output_schema.method: string - how it works, enough for a reader to explain it
methods: string - named methods, architectures or algorithms
models: string - models the work trains, evaluates or analyses, as named in the paper (e.g. a base checkpoint, a released reasoning model, a judge)
output_schema.one_liner: string - what the paper does, in one sentence, no hype
output_schema.problem: string - the problem it addresses and why it is open

relevance.<topic-slug>: string - why this matters for that specific topic

output_schema.results: string - headline numbers, on which benchmarks, against what

payload.title: ParoQuant: Pairwise Rotation Quantization for Efficient Reasoning LLM Inference

contributions: ParoQuant, combining hardware-efficient pairwise Givens rotations with channel-wise scaling for outlier-robust quantization
co-designed inference kernels maximizing GPU efficiency at low overhead
2.4% average accuracy improvement over AWQ on reasoning tasks under weight-only quantization, at <10% overhead
result.limitations: Not stated in the fetched abstract beyond the weight-only-quantization comparison setting; comparison to weight-activation quantization is only described as 'comparable,' with no numeric detail retrieved.
result.method: Introduces ParoQuant, combining hardware-efficient, optimizable independent Givens (pairwise) rotations with channel-wise scaling to even out magnitude differences across channels and narrow the dynamic range within each quantization group, paired with co-designed inference kernels that maximize GPU efficiency while keeping computational overhead minimal.
result.one_liner: ParoQuant is a post-training weight quantization method for reasoning LLMs that uses pairwise Givens rotations plus channel-wise scaling to even out per-channel outlier magnitudes, achieving 2.4% higher accuracy than AWQ on reasoning tasks at under 10% inference overhead.
result.problem: Post-training quantization reduces LLM memory and inference cost but outlier weight/activation magnitudes cause substantial quantization error and accuracy loss, and this is especially damaging for reasoning models because errors compound through long chains of reasoning steps; existing outlier-handling methods either handle outliers inadequately or impose heavy inference cost.

relevance.overthinking: Directly relevant as a complementary efficiency lever: it notes explicitly that quantization errors compound through long reasoning chains, making reasoning models especially sensitive to outlier-induced quantization error -- tying model-compression fidelity to the same long-generation cost that reasoning-length-focused overthinking mitigations address from the other direction (shortening the chain rather than cheapening each step).

result.results: Under weight-only quantization, ParoQuant achieves an average 2.4% accuracy improvement over AWQ on reasoning tasks with under 10% inference overhead, and performs comparably to leading weight-activation quantization approaches.
